opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it looks sudden from the outside, but from the inside it's a lot of things that had been building for a while and finally lined up.

The first piece is that coding is an unusually good domain for reinforcement learning. With most tasks it's hard to tell whether the model did a good job. With code you can often just run it. Does it compile, do the tests pass, does it do what the spec says? That gives you a verifiable reward signal, and once reasoning models became a thing, where the model can think for a long time, try something, check it, and back up, coding was where that paid off first and most dramatically.

The second piece is that the bottleneck moved. For a while the models were smart enough to write a function but couldn't work in a real codebase. They didn't have the context, they couldn't navigate files, run commands, or read error messages and iterate. A lot of the recent jump is really about agency: longer context, better tool use, and the scaffolding around the model, so it can operate like an engineer over many steps instead of one-shotting a snippet. Each of those improvements is incremental, but they multiply, so when they all cross a threshold together it feels like a step change.

The third piece is the economics. Coding is where the labs themselves feel the value most directly. Their own engineers use these tools all day, so there's a very tight feedback loop. People know exactly what's broken, and there's a huge commercial pull because developers will adopt something the week it gets better. That focuses a lot of effort.

So my mental model is less "something magical happened" and more that we had a domain with cheap verification, a technique, RL on reasoning, that's great at exploiting cheap verification, and an industry that was highly motivated to push on it. Put those together and progress on coding moves faster than almost anywhere else.

The interesting question going forward is how much of that transfers. Some of it, the long-horizon planning, the tool use, the ability to check your own work, should generalize. But domains where you can't easily verify the answer are going to be harder, and I think that's where you'll see a lot of the research effort go next.

r001.rationale: The response says incremental improvements multiply and crossing a threshold makes progress feel like a step change. It does not explain the takeoff as exponential capability growth, so the full criterion is not communicated.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the word "sudden" is doing a lot of work in that question, and I'd push back on it a little. From the outside it looked like coding went from a party trick to something real in about eighteen months. From the inside, it looked like a fairly smooth curve that happened to cross a usability threshold.

Here's what I mean. If you plot the fraction of real engineering tasks a model can finish end to end, that number was climbing steadily the whole time. But the product experience is not linear in that number. At thirty percent, the model is a distraction, because you spend more time cleaning up than you saved. At seventy or eighty percent, it flips. Now it's worth handing off work and reviewing the result. The underlying capability moved a few points a quarter, but the user's experience went from "this is annoying" to "I can't work without this." That discontinuity is in the product, not in the model.

The second thing is that coding is close to an ideal domain for the way we train these systems. You have a verifiable signal. The code compiles or it doesn't, the tests pass or they don't. That lets you do reinforcement learning at scale without needing a human in the loop to say whether the answer was good. Math has the same property. Once labs figured out how to make RL on reasoning work, coding was the first place it was going to show up, because the feedback is so clean and so cheap. It's not that coding is magically easy for models. It's that we could pour compute into it in a way we still can't for, say, writing a good essay or running a negotiation.

Third, there's a reasoning piece. The earlier models were basically pattern completing. They could write a function that looked right. The newer ones can hold a plan, run something, look at the error, and revise. That shift, from one-shot generation to an agent that iterates against the environment, is what made longer tasks tractable. A lot of what people perceive as a capability jump is really a jump in how long the model can stay coherent on a task before it drifts. That number has been roughly doubling every several months, and when the horizon goes from five minutes of work to a couple of hours, that's the difference between autocomplete and a junior engineer.

So my honest read is that nothing sudden happened in the research. The scaling kept working, RL on verifiable tasks started working, and agentic scaffolding matured. Those three compounded, and coding was simply the first domain where the compounding became obvious to everyone. The interesting question is which domain is next, and my guess is it's whichever one someone figures out how to make verifiable.

r001.rationale: The response explains a usability threshold that makes the impact feel nonlinear, but describes underlying capability as steadily increasing by a few points each quarter. It does not explain the takeoff as exponential capability growth.

astra-6.text:
I think it looks more sudden from the outside than it feels when you’re watching the models improve. Coding has this interesting property where you can get steadily better at individual pieces, but until you can put enough of those pieces together reliably, the system still requires a lot of supervision. Once you cross that threshold, it starts to feel qualitatively different: you can hand off a task instead of asking for help with a line of code.

And coding gives you a way to check your work. You can run the program, run tests, look at the errors, and try again. So improvements in the model get amplified by giving it the tools and the opportunity to iterate. It doesn’t have to get everything right on the first attempt.

I’d distinguish that from saying software engineering is solved. Figuring out what to build, understanding an existing system, and knowing whether a change actually meets the user’s needs are still hard. But the shift from generating code to completing a task is a big deal, and I think that’s a lot of what people are reacting to.

r001.rationale: The response describes steady improvements accumulating until a reliability threshold makes coding feel qualitatively different, but it does not characterize capability growth as exponential.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it looks sudden because coding has crossed a threshold where a lot of improvements become useful at once. A model that gets you part of the way there can be an interesting demo, but you still spend a lot of time figuring out what it got wrong. Once it can make a change, run the tests, interpret the failure, and try again, you can hand it a much larger piece of work.

Coding is particularly well suited to that loop because there’s feedback. You can execute the code. Tests don’t tell you everything, but they give the model a way to check its work. So improvements in reasoning and improvements in the tools reinforce each other.

I’d distinguish that from saying software engineering is solved. Understanding what someone actually wants, choosing the right abstractions, and maintaining a large system are still difficult. But when the model can stay on task long enough to produce something useful, the experience changes pretty dramatically. The underlying progress can be gradual while the change in how people use it feels sudden.

r001.rationale: The response explains the sudden shift as gradual progress crossing a usefulness threshold, but does not describe the capability growth as exponential.
